title: At the UN, World Leaders Confront War, Runaway AI, and Climate Shocks
summary:
Under a cloud of wars and bitter divisions, world leaders are meeting at the United Nations this week to confront a daunting list of global crises: escalating conflicts, climate shocks, rising prices, and new fears that runaway artificial intelligence could threaten humanity.

The annual high-level gathering at the UN's 193-member body will focus on what can be done about global warming, growing inequality, and economic shocks from blocked shipping routes and supply chains. The future of the UN itself is also on the agenda. At 81, its most powerful body — the Security Council — still gives veto power to the victorious nations of World War II: the U.S., Russia, China, Britain, and France. Member nations have agreed to a reform package, but reform is easier said than done.

About 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak starting Tuesday. U.S. President Donald Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron will address the assembly after Secretary-General Antonio Guterres delivers his opening "state of the world" address. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian speak Wednesday. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addresses the assembly Thursday.

For a second year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas won't attend because the U.S. refused him a visa. He will speak by video instead. China's President Xi Jinping is meeting Trump in Washington on Wednesday but skipping the UN gathering — some diplomats call it a snub. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian President Narendra Modi are also not coming.

France's UN ambassador, Jerome Bonnafont, said it is "extremely critical" for leaders to support the UN as a place for dialogue. "We believe in multilateralism," he said, "and we believe that the high-level week is the occasion for countries to reaffirm that they prefer cooperation and dialogue to confrontation."

The UN has had a tough year. The U.S. failed to pay billions in dues, leaving finances rocky. Recently, the U.S. paid $725 million to keep its General Assembly vote. Expert Richard Gowan said the UN is no longer "in freefall" but "stuck in an open-ended or permanent crisis."
why_it_matters: The UN is the main forum where small and large countries meet as equals, so its gridlock and money problems decide whether the world can act together on climate, AI and wars. For today's teenagers — who will inherit a system built in 1945 — the debate over who gets a veto and who pays the bills is really a debate about whose problems get solved.

background_read: The United Nations was founded in 1945 by countries that had just fought World War II, and today it has 193 member states. Its most powerful arm, the Security Council, gives permanent seats — and veto power — to five wartime victors: the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France. Because any one of them can block a resolution, critics say the Council freezes whenever a conflict involves one of its own members, and countries such as India, Brazil, Germany and Japan have long campaigned for permanent seats of their own.

Every September, heads of state and government gather in New York for the high-level 'general debate', opened by the Secretary-General — Antonio Guterres has held that role since 2017 — with a 'state of the world' address. Among those scheduled this year are Emmanuel Macron (France's president since 2017) and Volodymyr Zelenskyy (Ukraine's president since 2019). Mahmoud Abbas leads the Palestinian Authority and represents Palestinians at the UN as a non-member observer state.

The UN's regular budget comes from member dues, and the United States is the largest single contributor — so when Washington withholds payments, the whole organisation feels it. Under the UN Charter, countries that fall far behind can lose their vote in the General Assembly, which is why a recent $725 million payment mattered so much. That mix of money troubles, veto gridlock and absent leaders is what makes this year's gathering a test of whether multilateralism still works.

perspectives.description: France's ambassador Jerome Bonnafont argues the high-level week is 'extremely critical' because it is the one moment when almost every country can sit at the same table and choose dialogue over confrontation. From this view, even a flawed UN is better than no forum at all — especially for smaller nations that would otherwise have no stage.

They point to the absences: Xi Jinping, Putin and Modi are staying away, the U.S. has withheld billions in dues, and a single veto can paralyse the Security Council. If the most powerful leaders skip the meeting and the biggest contributor pays late, the organisation looks less like a world parliament and more like a talking shop.

The Security Council's structure is a photograph of 1945: it rewards the powers that won World War II, not the world of today. Experts like Richard Gowan note the UN is no longer 'in freefall' but 'stuck in an open-ended or permanent crisis' — a pattern that has repeated through the Cold War and after, where the institution bends but rarely breaks.

A reform package has been agreed in principle, but changing veto rights requires the very powers that hold them to agree — an almost circular problem. The next tests will be whether new issues like artificial intelligence and climate finance can be governed multilaterally, and whether absent giants like China and Russia can be drawn back into the room.
